e-methanol 18.7 Mt, biomethanol 13.1 Mt, blue methanol 8.1 Mt, together 39.9 Mt, from 190 projects
solution: The first option. As of 11/2024 the database counts 190 renewable methanol projects globally, with announced 2030 capacities of 18.7 Mt of e-methanol, 13.1 Mt of biomethanol and 8.1 Mt of blue (low-carbon) methanol, i.e. 39.9 Mt in total. The pipeline chart shows how steeply that is meant to ramp: 0.8 Mt in 2023, 1.0 in 2024, 4.5 in 2025, 11.3 in 2026, 24.1 in 2027, 34.3 in 2028, 38.3 in 2029 and 39.9 Mt in 2030. Two reality checks. First, only about 50 % of these projects are judged to have a higher realisation probability, so halve the figure. Second, even the full 39.9 Mt would be about 40 % of today's 98 Mt/a conventional methanol market - ambitious, but for once an announced pipeline of the same order of magnitude as the existing market rather than a hundred times smaller, which is why methanol is often called the most realistic of the derivatives.

prompt: What is a LOHC? Name the molecule pairs the lecture gives, the key figures, and the two process steps with their conditions.
solution:
A liquid organic hydrogen carrier is a liquid organic compound - a "carrier oil" - that can reversibly bond hydrogen. It is organic, but there is no CO2 release, because the carbon stays in the carrier molecule and the carrier is reused: it is a container, not a fuel. LOHCs are viscous liquids with flow characteristics similar to mineral oil, and many of them are by-products of oil refining.

The pairs, always given as lean form / rich form: methylcyclohexane MCH with toluol TOL; dibenzyltoluol H0-DBT with perhydro-dibenzyltoluol H18-DBT; benzyltoluol H0-BT (C14H14) with perhydro-benzyltoluol H12-BT (C14H26); and N-ethylcarbazole NEC with dodecahydro-N-ethylcarbazole DNEC. The number in the name counts the hydrogen atoms bound: H0-DBT is empty, H18-DBT is fully loaded with 18 hydrogen atoms, i.e. nine H2 molecules.

Key figures: energy density about 2 kWh/kg and 1.6 kWh/l, with a hydrogen content of 4 - 7 wt.% - the lowest of all the carriers, because the heavy carrier molecule has to be transported in both directions.

Process: exothermal hydrogenation at 30 - 50 bar and 150 - 200 °C in the exporting country, and endothermic dehydrogenation to release the hydrogen at about 250 - 400 °C, costing 9 - 14 kWh/kgH2, in the importing country. That asymmetry is the whole economics of LOHC: the heat is released where energy is cheap and required where energy is expensive.

prompt: In the LOHC pair dibenzyltoluol the hydrogen-lean form is written H0-DBT and the fully loaded, hydrogen-rich form is written ___.
solution: H18-DBT, perhydro-dibenzyltoluol. The number gives the hydrogen atoms bound to the carrier: H0-DBT is the empty carrier and H18-DBT carries 18 hydrogen atoms, i.e. nine molecules of H2 per carrier molecule, corresponding to about 6.2 wt.% hydrogen. The same convention appears in the other pairs: H0-BT (C14H14, benzyltoluol) and H12-BT (C14H26, perhydro-benzyltoluol) - note that C14H26 has twelve hydrogen atoms more than C14H14. Dibenzyltoluol is the industrially preferred carrier because it is a commercially available heat transfer oil, is not classified as hazardous, and has a very high boiling point, so it does not evaporate together with the released hydrogen.

prompt: Name the advantages of LOHCs as energy carriers and explain what makes the safety argument for LOHC stronger than for hydrogen or ammonia.
solution: LOHCs are easier to handle than hydrogen and ammonia because they are liquid at ambient conditions - no cryogenics, no pressure vessels. They allow the potential re-use of mineral oil infrastructure: tanker ships, rail and road transport and storage tanks, because the loaded carrier behaves like a mineral oil. They are hardly flammable and non-explosive, even when loaded with hydrogen, since the hydrogen is chemically bound in the molecule and cannot simply leak out. The carrier material is commercially available and reusable - it is shipped back empty and loaded again, so it is a working fluid rather than a consumable. And storage is loss-free, with no self-discharge: unlike liquid hydrogen with its 0.2 % per day boil-off, a loaded LOHC can stand in an ordinary tank for years without losing anything.\n\nThe safety argument is the strongest of these and it is worth stating precisely. Hydrogen is highly flammable over a very wide concentration range and ignites at extremely low energy; ammonia is toxic and caustic, so a release in a port is a public health event. A loaded LOHC is essentially a diesel-like oil: a leak is an environmental nuisance, not an explosion and not a toxic cloud, and it can be handled with the equipment, the standards and the trained personnel the oil industry already has. That is why the lecture's example company, Hydrogenious, targets shipping and small-scale container units - applications where the safety case and the permitting, not the energy density, decide whether the project happens.

prompt: Name the challenges of LOHCs as energy carriers and explain why the dehydrogenation step is the decisive weakness.
solution: Four challenges. First, the energy-intense, endothermal dehydrogenation process, which takes place in the energy importing country. Second, a lower energy density than hydrogen, ammonia and methanol: about 2 kWh/kg and 1.6 kWh/l, with only 4 - 7 wt.% hydrogen. Third, the dehydrogenation process is not mature. Fourth, further risks depend on the physical parameters of the chosen carrier oil - toxicity, viscosity, melting point and the behaviour of the degradation products differ from molecule to molecule, and the carrier slowly degrades over repeated cycles.\n\nDehydrogenation is decisive for three reasons. It costs 9 - 14 kWh/kgH2 at about 250 - 400 °C, roughly a third of the hydrogen's own energy content, and it demands that energy as high-temperature heat exactly where energy is expensive, in the importing country - whereas the exothermic hydrogenation releases its heat where energy is cheap and it is worth least. The temperature level is too high to be covered by the waste heat of a PEM fuel cell, so the plant must either burn part of the released hydrogen or find an external heat source. And the transport penalty compounds it: only 4 - 7 wt.% of the cargo is hydrogen, so a tanker carries roughly fifteen to twenty times as much carrier oil as hydrogen, and the empty carrier has to be shipped back, which doubles the shipping volume. That is why the lecture places LOHC at small demands and moderate distances rather than in the intercontinental bulk trade.

prompt: Slide 677 shows the cost surface from Reuß et al. (2019): the cost of hydrogen at the filling station as a function of hydrogen demand and of the average distance from the electrolyzer. Explain how the optimal supply chain changes across that surface and name the three regions.
solution:
The surface plots the cost of hydrogen in EUR/kg - roughly 7.2 up to more than 10.4 on the colour scale - over two axes: the demand of hydrogen, 0 to 100 t/day, and the average distance from the electrolyzer to the filling station, 0 to 500 km. It is divided into three regions, each labelled with the cheapest combination of storage and transport.

LOHC-Tank / LOHC-Truck occupies the low-demand corner, and that corner is also the most expensive part of the surface, above 10 EUR/kg. At small throughput the fixed costs of a cavern or of a pipeline cannot be spread over enough kilograms, so the chain with the lowest capital intensity wins even though it is thermodynamically the poorest.

GH2-Cavern / GH2-Truck takes the middle of the surface: once the demand justifies leaching a salt cavern, gaseous hydrogen stored underground and delivered in tube trailers is cheapest, as long as the distances stay moderate.

GH2-Cavern / GH2-Pipe takes the high-demand, long-distance corner, which is also the cheapest area overall, down to about 5 - 7 EUR/kg. A pipeline is almost pure fixed cost with a negligible marginal cost per kilogram, so it needs both high utilisation and a long distance before it beats trucking.

The three bullets on the slide summarise exactly this: LOHC for smaller demands; transport by pipeline only for long distances combined with high demands; storage in an underground cavern for larger quantities. The economic logic is the one already used for gas and oil in this lecture - the choice between transport modes is a trade-off between fixed and variable costs, so the decisive variables are throughput and distance, not the technology as such.

prompt: Hydrogenious LOHC Technologies, the global market leader in LOHC technology, is a German company from Erlangen founded in 2013 as a spin-off from the FAU; the carrier material it uses is ___.
solution: Benzyltoluene (benzyltoluol), i.e. the H0-BT / H12-BT pair, chosen over dibenzyltoluol because of its lower viscosity and lower melting point, which suits the small-scale container units the company builds. Milestones from the slide: in 2017 the world's first LOHC plant for the storage and release of hydrogen, delivered to a US-based customer; in 2021 the joint venture "Hydrogenious LOHC Maritime" with the shipping company Østensjø Rederi in Norway, to establish LOHC in the shipping industry; the world's largest plant for storing green hydrogen in LOHCs at CHEMPARK Dormagen in North Rhine-Westphalia, with a capacity of 1,800 tH2 per year; and a hydrogen release plant in Bavaria with the same capacity of 1,800 tH2 per year, planned for 2028. Note the pairing of a storage plant in the Rhineland with a release plant in Bavaria: that is the LOHC business model in miniature - load the oil where the hydrogen is produced, move it with ordinary rail and road tankers, and release the hydrogen where the customer sits.
